claim: Sensory hair cells receive near constant stimulation by omnipresent auditory and vestibular stimuli.
source: Sensory hair cells receive near constant stimulation by omnipresent auditory and vestibular stimuli.
evidence: This is a general statement about hair cell function presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but draws on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Hair cells require steady ATP production to detect and encode auditory and vestibular stimuli.
source: To detect and encode these stimuli, hair cells require steady ATP production, which can be accompanied by a buildup of mitochondrial byproducts called reactive oxygen species (ROS).
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about hair cell metabolism.

claim: ATP production in hair cells can be accompanied by a buildup of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: To detect and encode these stimuli, hair cells require steady ATP production, which can be accompanied by a buildup of mitochondrial byproducts called reactive oxygen species (ROS).
evidence: This is stated as a known consequence of ATP production and is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: ROS buildup sensitizes hair cells to ototoxic insults, including the antibiotic neomycin.
source: ROS buildup is thought to sensitize hair cells to ototoxic insults, including the antibiotic neomycin.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis that is tested and supported by the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Neurotransmission is a major driver of ATP production and ROS buildup in neurons.
source: Work in neurons has shown that neurotransmission is a major driver of ATP production and ROS buildup.
evidence: This statement references prior work in neurons as background for the current study.

claim: Chronic block of neurotransmission enhances hair-cell survival when challenged with the ototoxin neomycin.
source: We find that chronic block of neurotransmission enhances hair-cell survival when challenged with the ototoxin neomycin.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Reduction in ototoxin susceptibility is accompanied by reduced mitochondrial activity in hair cells with blocked neurotransmission.
source: This reduction in ototoxin susceptibility is accompanied by reduced mitochondrial activity, likely due to a reduced ATP demand.
evidence: This finding is supported by TMRE and JC-1 measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mitochondrial oxidation and ROS buildup are reduced when neurotransmission is blocked.
source: In addition, we show that mitochondrial oxidation and ROS buildup are reduced when neurotransmission is blocked.
evidence: This is supported by CellROX, MitoSOX, and MitoTimer data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The synaptic vesicle cycle rather than presynaptic- or mitochondrial-calcium influx contributes most significantly to metabolic stress in hair cells.
source: Mechanistically, we find that it is the synaptic vesicle cycle rather than presynaptic- or mitochondrial-calcium influx that contributes most significantly to this metabolic stress.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by comparing cav1.3a and otofb mutants, and by pharmacological experiments shown in Figures 2 and 7.

claim: Over time, neurotransmission causes ROS buildup that increases the susceptibility of hair cells to ototoxins.
source: Our results comprehensively indicate that, over time, neurotransmission causes ROS buildup that increases the susceptibility of hair cells to ototoxins.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence throughout the manuscript.

claim: Hair cells contain specialized synapses that work near constantly to convert sensory stimuli into electrical signals.
source: Hair cells contain specialized synapses that work near constantly to convert sensory stimuli into electrical signals (McPherson, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In hair cells, neurotransmission requires extensive amounts of energy, similar to neurons.
source: Similar to neurons, in hair cells, neurotransmission requires extensive amounts of energy (Rangaraju et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work in neurons.

claim: Energy demands in hair cells are met by ATP produced via mitochondrial respiration.
source: These energy demands are met by ATP produced via mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: This is a statement of established cellular metabolism.

claim: Mitochondrial respiration is accompanied by the production of cytotoxic reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Mitochondrial respiration is accompanied by the production of cytotoxic reactive oxygen species (ROS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial metabolism.

claim: Elevated levels of ROS result in an accumulation of oxidative stress that renders neurons and hair cells more susceptible to insults and can ultimately lead to cell death.
source: Elevated levels of ROS result in an accumulation of oxidative stress that renders neurons and hair cells more susceptible to insults and can ultimately lead to cell death (Singh et al., 2019; Wong and Ryan, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In humans, hair-cell death or damage can result in irreversible hearing loss.
source: In humans, hair-cell death or damage can result in irreversible hearing loss (Mittal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Hair cells rely on two critical, metabolically demanding processes: mechanosensation and synaptic transmission.
source: To convert sensory stimuli into neuronal signals, hair cells rely on two critical, metabolically demanding processes: mechanosensation and synaptic transmission (McPherson, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Deflection of the mechanosensory bundle opens mechanoelectrical transducer (MET) channels which allows potassium and calcium into the cell.
source: Deflection of the mechanosensory bundle opens nonspecific cation channels known as mechanoelectrical transducer (MET) channels which allows potassium and calcium into the cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair cell mechanotransduction.

claim: MET channel function requires a calcium gradient in the mechanosensory bundle.
source: MET channel function requires a calcium gradient in the mechanosensory bundle; maintenance of this gradient requires the plasma-membrane calcium-ATPase (PMCA) and is thought to pose a large energy demand (Dumont and Gillespie, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Maintenance of the calcium gradient in the mechanosensory bundle requires the plasma-membrane calcium-ATPase (PMCA) and is thought to pose a large energy demand.
source: MET channel function requires a calcium gradient in the mechanosensory bundle; maintenance of this gradient requires the plasma-membrane calcium-ATPase (PMCA) and is thought to pose a large energy demand (Dumont and Gillespie, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MET channel-dependent cationic influx depolarizes the cell and triggers synaptic transmission at the base of the hair cell.
source: MET channel-dependent cationic influx depolarizes the cell and triggers synaptic transmission at the base of the hair cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair cell physiology.

claim: Depolarization leads to the opening of basal, voltage-gated Cav1.3 calcium channels at the hair-cell presynapse.
source: Depolarization leads to the opening of basal, voltage-gated Cav1.3 calcium channels at the hair-cell presynapse (Brandt et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Calcium influx through Cav1.3 channels is detected by the calcium sensor Otoferlin.
source: This calcium influx is detected by the calcium sensor Otoferlin (Roux et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Otoferlin is required to couple calcium influx with exocytosis and ultimately mediate the release of glutamate-containing vesicles onto the afferent neurons.
source: Otoferlin is required to couple calcium influx with exocytosis and ultimately mediate the release of glutamate-containing vesicles onto the afferent neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: The metabolic demands of mechanosensation have been implicated in increased susceptibility to ototoxic insults.
source: Although the metabolic demands of mechanosensation have been implicated in increased susceptibility to ototoxic insults (Pickett et al., 2018), the contribution of neurotransmission to this process is unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: caV1.3a zebrafish mutants exhibit impaired hair-cell function as well as defects in hearing and balance.
source: Previous studies have shown that caV1.3a zebrafish mutants exhibit impaired hair-cell function as well as defects in hearing and balance (Sidi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Hearing and balance defects were observed in zebrafish following morpholino knockdown of Otoferlin mRNA in hair cells.
source: Hearing and balance defects were also observed in zebrafish following morpholino knockdown of Otoferlin mRNA in hair cells (Chatterjee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Both otofa and otofb are present in hair cells in the zebrafish inner ear, while only otofb is present in hair cells of the lateral-line system.
source: Analysis of zebrafish otof morphants revealed that both otofa and otofb are present in hair cells in the zebrafish inner ear, while only otofb is present in hair cells of the lateral-line system.
evidence: This is based on prior morpholino analysis referenced in the text.

claim: Otoferlin immunolabel is absent in the lateral-line hair cells of otofb mutants.
source: In line with previous work, we found that Otoferlin immunolabel is absent in the lateral-line hair cells of otofb mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-D; Varshney et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microphonic potentials are qualitatively reduced in Cav1.3a-deficient neuromasts.
source: Previous work has shown that microphonic potentials (summed potentials dependent on mechanotransduction) are qualitatively reduced in Cav1.3a-deficient neuromasts (Nicolson et al., 1998; Trapani and Nicolson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The magnitude, slope, and duration of GCaMP6s signals in apical mechanosensory bundles were comparable to those observed in sibling controls in both caV1.3a and otofb mutants in response to a 500 ms fluid-jet stimulus.
source: In response to a 500 ms fluid-jet stimulus, we observed that the magnitude, slope, and duration of GCaMP6s signals in apical mechanosensory bundles were comparable to those observed in sibling controls in both caV1.3a and otofb mutants (Figure 1E–F', Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1E-F' and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The resting GCaMP6s intensity in hair bundles of caV1.3a mutants tended to be higher relative to controls.
source: We found that although it was not significantly different, the resting GCaMP6s intensity in hair bundles of caV1.3a mutants tended to be higher relative to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A); no difference was observed in otofb mutants.
evidence: This is supported by baseline calcium measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: GCaMP6s responses returned to baseline faster in caV1.3a mutants relative to controls.
source: In addition, we also observed that GCaMP6s responses returned to baseline faster in caV1.3a mutants relative to controls (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: It is possible that caV1.3a mutants have subtle defects in mechanotransduction.
source: Because the resting calcium levels in hair bundles are higher in caV1.3a mutants and the recovery of the GCaMP6s responses is faster, it is possible that caV1.3a mutants have subtle defects in mechanotransduction.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the calcium imaging data.

claim: Both Cav1.3a- and Otofb-deficient hair cells exhibit largely normal evoked mechanotransduction.
source: Overall, our GCaMP6s measurements indicate that both Cav1.3a- and Otofb-deficient hair cells exhibit largely normal evoked mechanotransduction.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Eliminating hair-cell mechanosensation could render hair cells more resistant to cellular stressors.
source: This result is important in light of previous work that found eliminating hair-cell mechanosensation could render hair cells more resistant to cellular stressors (Pickett et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The magnitude, slope, duration, and recovery of GCaMP6s signals in otofb mutants was unchanged compared to controls during a 500 ms stimulus at the base of hair cells.
source: Our measurements at the base of hair cells revealed that during a 500 ms stimulus, the magnitude, slope, duration, and recovery of GCaMP6s signals in otofb mutants was unchanged compared to controls (Figure 1G–H', Figure 1—figure supplement 2J-L).
evidence: This is supported by presynaptic calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1G-H' and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: cav1.3a mutants completely lacked presynaptic-calcium responses.
source: In contrast, cav1.3a mutants completely lacked presynaptic-calcium responses (Figure 1G–H').
evidence: This is supported by presynaptic calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1G-H'.

claim: Resting calcium levels were significantly reduced in caV1.3a mutants compared to controls at the base of hair cells.
source: We also examined the resting GCaMP6s intensity at the base of hair cells and found that, consistent with a loss of CaV1.3-channel activity, resting calcium levels were significantly reduced in caV1.3a mutants compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I); no difference was observed in otofb mutants.
evidence: This is supported by baseline calcium measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2I.

claim: CaV1.3 channels but not Otoferlin are required for presynaptic-calcium influx in lateral-line hair cells.
source: Our presynaptic measurements indicate that, similar to results obtained in mice, CaV1.3 channels but not Otoferlin are required for presynaptic-calcium influx in lateral-line hair cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the presynaptic calcium imaging data in Figure 1G-H' and comparison to prior work in mice.

claim: Both caV1.3a and otofb mutants lack evoked exocytosis.
source: Upon hair-cell stimulation, we observed no increase in SypHy fluorescence in either mutant, revealing that both mutants lack evoked exocytosis (Figure 1I–J').
evidence: This is supported by SypHy imaging data shown in Figure 1I-J'.

claim: The lack of exocytosis in zebrafish hair cells agrees with previously published data collected from the auditory system in Cav1.3 and Otof mouse mutants.
source: This lack of exocytosis in zebrafish hair cells agrees with previously published data collected from the auditory system in Cav1.3 and Otof mouse mutants (Brandt et al., 2003; Roux et al., 2006).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to prior work in mice.

claim: Residual evoked and spontaneous exocytosis has been observed in the vestibular system of Otof mouse mutants.
source: While Otoferlin is essential for exocytosis in auditory hair cells, residual evoked and spontaneous exocytosis has been observed in the vestibular system of Otof mouse mutants (Dulon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Very few spontaneous afferent spikes were detected in caV1.3a mutants.
source: In agreement with previously published data, we detected very few spontaneous afferent spikes in caV1.3a mutants (Trapani and Nicolson, 2011; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F and citation to prior work.

claim: Very few spontaneous afferent spikes were observed in otofb mutants.
source: We also examined otofb mutants and similarly observed very few spontaneous afferent spikes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F; sibling: 399.0±79.7, caV1.3a: 5.9±2.9, otofb: 4.2±1.2 spikes per min).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: In lateral-line hair cells, both CaV1.3 channels and Otoferlin are essential for evoked and spontaneous exocytosis.
source: Overall, our SypHy and electrophysiology results indicate that in lateral-line hair cells, both CaV1.3 channels and Otoferlin are essential for evoked and spontaneous exocytosis.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the SypHy and electrophysiology data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Both caV1.3a and otofb mutants have relatively normal mechanosensitive function.
source: Together our comprehensive functional assessment of caV1.3a and otofb mutants revealed that both mutants have relatively normal mechanosensitive function.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the functional imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: In lateral-line hair cells Cav1.3 channels are required for both presynaptic calcium influx and exocytosis while Otoferlin is only required for exocytosis.
source: In lateral-line hair cells Cav1.3 channels are required for both presynaptic calcium influx and exocytosis while Otoferlin is only required for exocytosis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the functional imaging and electrophysiology data in Figure 1.

claim: caV1.3a and otofb mutants impair overlapping aspects of hair-cell neurotransmission.
source: Importantly, caV1.3a and otofb mutants impair overlapping aspects of hair-cell neurotransmission and are useful models to explore the relationship between neurotransmission and metabolic stress.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the functional characterization in Figure 1.

claim: The energy demands of neurotransmission can lead to a buildup of cytotoxic metabolic byproducts and render neurons more susceptible to insults.
source: In neurons, the energy demands of neurotransmission can lead to a buildup of cytotoxic metabolic byproducts and render cells more susceptible to insults (Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work in neurons.

claim: Hair cells are acutely susceptible to many stressors, including ototoxins such as aminoglycoside antibiotics.
source: Hair cells are acutely susceptible to many stressors, including ototoxins such as aminoglycoside antibiotics (Bitner-Glindzicz and Rahman, 2007; Coffin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: At all concentrations tested (75, 100, and 200 µM neomycin), the mean % hair-cell survival for cav1.3a and otofb mutants was significantly higher compared to sibling controls.
source: At all concentrations tested, the mean % hair-cell survival for cav1.3a and otofb mutants was significantly higher compared to sibling controls.
evidence: This is supported by neomycin survival data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: The neurotransmission defects in cav1.3a and otofb mutants impart resistance to neomycin.
source: These results indicate that the neurotransmission defects in cav1.3a and otofb mutants impart resistance to neomycin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the neomycin survival data in Figure 2.

claim: Aminoglycosides enter hair cells primarily via mechanosensitive ion channels in hair bundles.
source: To exert their toxicity, aminoglycoside antibiotics such as neomycin and gentamicin enter hair cells primarily via mechanosensitive ion channels in hair bundles (Figure 1D; Alharazneh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Blocking the MET channel is an effective method of protecting hair cells from aminoglycoside-induced cell death.
source: Based on this premise, studies have established that blocking the MET channel is an effective method of protecting hair cells from aminoglycoside-induced cell death (Alharazneh et al., 2011; Kenyon et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neurotransmission-deficient hair cells are protected from neomycin despite largely normal MET channel function as well as normal levels of neomycin accumulation and rates of neomycin entry.
source: However, in our study we found that neurotransmission-deficient hair cells are protected despite largely normal MET channel function as well as normal levels of neomycin accumulation and rates of neomycin entry (Figures 1 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by functional imaging data in Figure 1 and neomycin uptake data in Figure 3.

claim: The protective effects of blocking neurotransmission are not a result of augmented neomycin clearance.
source: Furthermore, our data indicates that the protective effects of blocking neurotransmission are not a result of augmented neomycin clearance (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by neomycin clearance data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The pathology underlying aminoglycoside exposure extends beyond the kinetics of uptake, accumulation, and clearance.
source: Thus, we show that the pathology underlying aminoglycoside exposure extends beyond the kinetics of uptake, accumulation, and clearance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the neomycin uptake and clearance data in Figure 3.

claim: After entering the hair cell, aminoglycosides rapidly build up in the cytoplasm.
source: After entering the hair cell, aminoglycosides rapidly build up in the cytoplasm (Alharazneh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the cytosol, aminoglycosides can interact with the plasma membrane and can accumulate in organelles such as the ER, mitochondria, and lysosomes.
source: In the cytosol, aminoglycosides can interact with the plasma membrane and can accumulate in organelles such as the ER, mitochondria, and lysosomes (Hailey et al., 2017; Hashino et al., 1997; Steyger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pharmacologically blocking aminoglycoside uptake into lysosomes exacerbates hair-cell death.
source: For example, work has shown that pharmacologically blocking aminoglycoside uptake into lysosomes exacerbates hair-cell death (Hailey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Lysosomes may play an important role in aminoglycoside degradation.
source: This indicates that lysosomes may play an important role in aminoglycoside degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited prior work.

claim: The uptake of neomycin into lysosomes is normal in the absence of neurotransmission.
source: In our study we found that the uptake of neomycin into lysosomes is normal in the absence of neurotransmission (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Neo-TR imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neurotransmission does not overtly modulate the lysosomal sequestration of neomycin.
source: This indicates that neurotransmission does not overtly modulate the lysosomal sequestration of neomycin and that more rapid or more efficient lysosomal packaging does not explain the protection observed in the absence of neurotransmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Neo-TR imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the lateral-line system, gentamicin treatment takes several hours to kill hair cells, as opposed to minutes in the case of neomycin.
source: For example, in the lateral-line system, gentamicin treatment takes several hours to kill hair cells, as opposed to minutes in the case of neomycin (Coffin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Compared to neomycin, gentamicin is much more rapidly packaged into lysosomes following its entry into hair cells.
source: It has been shown that, compared to neomycin, gentamicin is much more rapidly packaged into lysosomes following its entry into hair cells (Hailey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Rapid packaging of gentamicin into lysosomes is thought to be one reason gentamicin takes longer than neomycin to exert its pathological effects.
source: This rapid packaging is thought to be one reason gentamicin takes longer than neomycin to exert its pathological effects.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited prior work.

claim: Neomycin and gentamicin may initiate hair-cell death via different pathways.
source: In addition, studies have shown that these two aminoglycosides may initiate hair-cell death via different pathways (Coffin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Chronic loss of neurotransmission results in protection from both neomycin and gentamicin.
source: In our study we find that chronic loss of neurotransmission results in protection from both neomycin and gentamicin (Figure 2A–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-F), despite different time-courses of pathology, lysosomal packaging and cell-death pathways.
evidence: This is supported by neomycin and gentamicin survival data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Blocking neurotransmission provides a general form of otoprotection and may broadly protect against differently behaving ototoxic compounds or insults.
source: This suggests that blocking neurotransmission provides a general form of otoprotection and may broadly protect against differently behaving ototoxic compounds or insults.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the neomycin and gentamicin data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Maintaining metabolic homeostasis is thought to be critical to surviving ototoxin exposure.
source: In particular, maintaining metabolic homeostasis is thought to be critical to surviving ototoxin exposure (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ROS are byproducts of cellular metabolism and are normally present in low concentrations in all cell types.
source: ROS are byproducts of cellular metabolism and are normally present in low concentrations in all cell types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular metabolism.

claim: In hair cells, excess ROS buildup can lead to mitochondrial oxidation and trigger cell-death pathways – especially when hair cells are challenged with an ototoxin.
source: In hair cells, excess ROS buildup can lead to mitochondrial oxidation and trigger cell-death pathways – especially when hair cells are challenged with an ototoxin (Huang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The energy demands of neurotransmission promote cellular metabolism, which leads to a buildup of ROS and more oxidized mitochondria.
source: Our results indicate that the energy demands of neurotransmission promote cellular metabolism, which leads to a buildup of ROS and more oxidized mitochondria (Figures 5—7).
evidence: This is supported by ROS and mitochondrial oxidation data shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: Blocking neurotransmission can lessen metabolic side effects related to energy demands and protect hair cells from ototoxins.
source: Importantly we show that blocking neurotransmission can lessen metabolic side effects related to these energy demands and protect hair cells from ototoxins.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Both the electrical signaling and vesicle release required for neurotransmission require large amounts of ATP in neurons.
source: Studies in neurons suggest that both the electrical signaling and vesicle release required for neurotransmission require large amounts of ATP (reviewed in: Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review of prior work in neurons.

claim: Energy requirements of neurotransmission can increase the production of ROS and ultimately result in mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular vulnerability, and neuronal loss.
source: These energy requirements can increase the production of ROS and ultimately result in mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular vulnerability, and neuronal loss (Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra depend on the metabolically taxing, ATP-dependent process of calcium clearance for their pace-making function.
source: For example, dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra depend on the metabolically taxing, ATP-dependent process of calcium clearance for their pace-making function.
evidence: This is an example from prior work in neurons.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra accumulate ROS to a much greater extent than neighboring neurons.
source: These neurons have been shown to accumulate ROS to a much greater extent than neighboring neurons.
evidence: This is based on prior work in neurons.

claim: Mitochondrial pathology in dopaminergic neurons is thought to lead to cell death and the loss of dopaminergic neurons that underlies Parkinson's Disease.
source: This mitochondrial pathology is thought to lead to cell death and the loss of dopaminergic neurons that underlies Parkinson's Disease (Dias et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: High ATP demands in dopaminergic neurons are driven by the need to counterbalance the constant L-type calcium channel engagement that sets pacemaker function.
source: Interestingly, high ATP demands in these dopaminergic neurons are driven by the need to counterbalance the constant L-type calcium channel engagement that sets pacemaker function (Guzman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Activity related to L-type calcium channel (CaV1.3) function increases levels of ROS in hair cells.
source: In our work we also find that activity related to L-type calcium channel (CaV1.3) function increases levels of ROS in hair cells (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by MitoTimer data shown in Figure 6.

claim: After chronic pharmacological block of L-type calcium channels, dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra showed significantly lower mitochondrial oxidative stress.
source: In addition, after chronic pharmacological block of L-type calcium channels, dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra showed significantly lower mitochondrial oxidative stress (Guzman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work in neurons.

claim: Chronic block of CaV1.3 channels reduces mitochondrial activity, the amount of ROS, and mitochondrial oxidation in hair cells.
source: Similarly, in our study we found that chronic block of CaV1.3 channels reduces mitochondrial activity (Figure 5), the amount of ROS (Figure 5), and mitochondrial oxidation (Figure 6) in hair cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The metabolic demands associated with presynaptic calcium flux are high and potentially deleterious to both neuronal and hair-cell homeostasis and health.
source: Thus, the metabolic demands associated with presynaptic calcium flux are high and potentially deleterious to both neuronal and hair-cell homeostasis and health.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in the manuscript and comparison to prior work in neurons.

claim: The pathological effects of metabolic demands associated with presynaptic calcium flux represent a common theme in both hearing loss and neurodegenerative disease.
source: Furthermore, the pathological effects of these metabolic demands represent a common theme in both hearing loss and neurodegenerative disease (Singh et al., 2019; Wong and Ryan, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The synaptic vesicle cycle relies heavily on ATP produced by the mitochondria in neurons.
source: In addition to presynaptic calcium channel activity, work in neurons has demonstrated that the synaptic vesicle cycle relies heavily on ATP produced by the mitochondria (Pulido and Ryan, 2021; Rangaraju et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in neurons.

claim: Hair cells with intact CaV1.3 channel function but impaired synaptic vesicle exocytosis (Otofb deficient- and Dynole 34–2 treated-hair cells) were protected from aminoglycosides.
source: We found that hair cells with intact CaV1.3 channel function but impaired synaptic vesicle exocytosis (Otofb deficient- and Dynole 34–2 treated-hair cells) were protected from aminoglycosides (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by neomycin and gentamicin survival data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Hair cells with impaired exocytosis show a reduction in mitochondrial activity, oxidation and ROS levels.
source: In addition, hair cells with impaired exocytosis also show a reduction in mitochondrial activity (Figure 5), oxidation (Figure 6) and ROS levels (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Blocking CaV1.3 channel function in hair cells with impaired exocytosis did not confer any additional protection from neomycin.
source: Furthermore, blocking CaV1.3 channel function in hair cells with impaired exocytosis did not confer any additional protection from neomycin (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by neomycin survival data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In hair cells, the majority of the ATP required for neurotransmission is used by the synaptic vesicle cycle.
source: Together these results indicate that in hair cells, the majority of the ATP required for neurotransmission is used by the synaptic vesicle cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data comparing cav1.3a and otofb mutants shown in Figures 2, 5, 6, and 7.

claim: It is the compensatory endocytosis and synaptic vesicle replenishment following exocytosis that requires significant amounts of ATP in neurons.
source: In fact, work in neurons has shown that the synaptic vesicle cycle is an underappreciated consumer of ATP (Pulido and Ryan, 2021; Rangaraju et al., 2014). Within the synaptic vesicle cycle, work in neurons has shown that it is the compensatory endocytosis and synaptic vesicle replenishment following exocytosis that requires significant amounts of ATP.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in neurons.

claim: V-ATPases consume ATP in order to help fill vesicles with neurotransmitters such as glutamate and therefore represent a large metabolic burden.
source: Mechanistically, these ATP demands may arise at least in part from vacuolar-type ATPases (V-ATPases) which reside in synaptic vesicles (Pulido and Ryan, 2021). V-ATPases consume ATP in order to help fill vesicles with neurotransmitters such as glutamate and therefore represent a large metabolic burden.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and represents established knowledge about V-ATPase function.

claim: The synaptic vesicle cycle represents a source of metabolic stress that can impact cellular health.
source: Our work in hair cells and complementary work in neurons indicate that the synaptic vesicle cycle represents a source of metabolic stress that can impact cellular health.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in the manuscript and comparison to prior work in neurons.

claim: Mitochondria are thought to be a target of aminoglycosides.
source: Many studies on aminoglycoside ototoxicity point to mitochondrial involvement as they are thought to be a target of aminoglycosides (reviewed in: Foster and Tekin, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review of prior work.

claim: Hair-cell neurotransmission impacts mitochondria by promoting cellular metabolism, leading to a buildup of ROS and more oxidized mitochondria.
source: Our study highlights how hair-cell neurotransmission impacts mitochondria – promoting cellular metabolism, leading to a buildup of ROS and more oxidized mitochondria (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: When hair cells are challenged with aminoglycosides, mitochondrial pathology linked to neurotransmission and the targeting of aminoglycosides to the mitochondria synergize to initiate hair-cell death.
source: Under these conditions, when hair cells are challenged with aminoglycosides, mitochondrial pathology linked to neurotransmission and the targeting of aminoglycosides to the mitochondria synergize to initiate hair-cell death.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the data in the manuscript and prior knowledge about aminoglycoside toxicity.

claim: As hair cells mature and age, they accumulate more oxidized mitochondria.
source: We also show that as hair cells mature and age, they accumulate more oxidized mitochondria; block of neurotransmission dramatically reduces this oxidation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by MitoTimer data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Block of neurotransmission dramatically reduces mitochondrial oxidation that accumulates as hair cells age.
source: We also show that as hair cells mature and age, they accumulate more oxidized mitochondria; block of neurotransmission dramatically reduces this oxidation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by MitoTimer data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Presbycusis or age-related hearing loss (ARHL) is common in both animal models and humans.
source: Presbycusis or age-related hearing loss (ARHL) is common in both animal models and humans (Huang and Tang, 2010; Wang and Puel, 2020; Wong and Ryan, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In animal models, ARHL is associated with an accumulation of ROS and mitochondrial damage.
source: In animal models, ARHL is associated with an accumulation of ROS and mitochondrial damage.
evidence: This is based on prior work in animal models.

claim: Neurotransmission may be a critical link between aging and hair-cell vulnerability.
source: Our study suggests that neurotransmission may be a critical link between aging and hair-cell vulnerability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing ROS and mitochondrial oxidation accumulation over time.

claim: There is residual ROS accumulation and mitochondrial oxidation even in hair cells lacking neurotransmission.
source: Interestingly, we did observe residual ROS accumulation and mitochondrial oxidation even in hair cells lacking neurotransmission (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: In addition to neurotransmission, there are other factors that promote ROS accumulation and mitochondrial oxidation over time.
source: This indicates that in addition to neurotransmission, there are other factors that promote ROS accumulation and mitochondrial oxidation over time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of residual ROS in mutants.

claim: Without hair-cell neurotransmission hearing, balance, or lateral-line function are not possible.
source: But without hair-cell neurotransmission hearing, balance, or lateral-line function are not possible (Brandt et al., 2003; Chatterjee et al., 2015; Roux et al., 2006; Sidi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the lateral line, the majority of hair cells within neuromast organs are synaptically silent with no detectable evoked presynaptic calcium influx or vesicle fusion.
source: Interestingly, in our previous work we demonstrated that, in the lateral line, the majority of hair cells within neuromast organs are synaptically silent with no detectable evoked presynaptic calcium influx or vesicle fusion (Figures 1 and 4; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1 and 4 and citation to prior work.

claim: Synaptic silencing may be a protective mechanism that occurs in older, more mature hair cells where ROS levels and mitochondrial oxidation are elevated.
source: Given the relationship between hair-cell neurotransmission and metabolic stress, synaptic silencing may be a protective mechanism that occurs in older, more mature hair cells where ROS levels and mitochondrial oxidation are elevated (Pickett et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data and prior work.

claim: Synaptically silent hair cells are relatively older than synaptically active cells.
source: This is consistent with our present study where we show that synaptically silent hair cells are relatively older than synaptically active cells and are also more susceptible to neomycin (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI labeling and neomycin survival data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Synaptically silent hair cells are more susceptible to neomycin than synaptically active cells.
source: This is consistent with our present study where we show that synaptically silent hair cells are relatively older than synaptically active cells and are also more susceptible to neomycin (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by neomycin survival data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the lateral line, as hair cells age, synaptic silencing may serve as a mechanism to limit further ROS accumulation and mitochondrial oxidation.
source: Therefore, in the lateral line, as hair cells age, synaptic silencing may serve as a mechanism to limit further ROS accumulation and mitochondrial oxidation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data.

claim: A shift of neurotransmission from older to younger hair cells could limit the amount of damage hair cells accumulate and ultimately prevent widespread cell death, especially when neuromasts are faced with insults like neomycin.
source: A shift of neurotransmission from older to younger hair cells could limit the amount of damage hair cells accumulate and ultimately prevent widespread cell death, especially when neuromasts are faced with insults like neomycin.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data.

claim: Mammalian hair cells do not regenerate and must be maintained over a lifetime.
source: Such a mechanism would be extremely advantageous as mammalian hair cells do not regenerate and must be maintained over a lifetime.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian hair cells.

claim: Proper management of metabolic stress including ROS production and mitochondrial oxidation is critical for hair-cell health and resistance to ototoxins.
source: Overall, our study shows that proper management of metabolic stress including ROS production and mitochondrial oxidation is critical for hair-cell health and resistance to ototoxins.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data in the manuscript.

claim: Over time, hair-cell neurotransmission increases ROS production and mitochondrial oxidation resulting in increased vulnerability to aminoglycosides.
source: Furthermore, we find that, over time, hair-cell neurotransmission increases ROS production and mitochondrial oxidation resulting in increased vulnerability to aminoglycosides.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data in the manuscript.

claim: Aging-associated increase in vulnerability may shed light on presbycusis and the processes that lead to hearing loss with age.
source: This aging-associated increase in vulnerability may shed light on presbycusis and the processes that lead to hearing loss with age.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Acute isradipine treatment (10 min preincubation + 30 min co-incubation with neomycin) resulted in no change in hair cell survival compared to DMSO-treated controls.
source: For this experiment we preincubated larvae in 10 µM isradipine for 10 min, followed by a 30 min co-incubation with neomycin. After acute isradipine treatment, we observed no change in survival with a mean % hair-cell survival comparable to DMSO-treated controls (Figure 2F, 5-6 dpf).
evidence: This is supported by neomycin survival data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: 24 hr and 48 hr isradipine incubations prior to neomycin treatment significantly augmented hair-cell survival.
source: Here, we applied 10 µM isradipine to larvae at 4 dpf for 24 hr or at 3 dpf for 48 hrs prior to 100 µM neomycin treatment at 5 dpf. In contrast to our acute isradipine application, both of the longer 24 and 48 hr isradipine incubations significantly augmented hair-cell survival after neomycin treatment (Figure 2G-H, 5 dpf).
evidence: This is supported by neomycin survival data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: A relatively long (~24 hr) block of presynaptic calcium influx can confer significant resistance to neomycin.
source: This indicates that a relatively long (~24 hr) block of presynaptic calcium influx can confer significant resistance to neomycin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the isradipine pretreatment data in Figure 2G-H.

claim: 2.5 µM Dynole 34–2 treatment did not impair evoked mechanotransduction or presynaptic calcium influx compared to DMSO-treated controls.
source: Using calcium imaging, we found that 2.5 µM Dynole 34–2 treatment did not impair evoked mechanotransduction or presynaptic calcium influx compared to DMSO-treated controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: After a 10-min treatment with 2.5 µM Dynole 34–2, the number of spontaneous spikes recorded from lateral-line afferents was significantly reduced.
source: Importantly, we found that after a 10-min treatment with 2.5 µM Dynole 34–2, the number of spontaneous spikes recorded from lateral-line afferents was significantly reduced (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Dynole 34–2 specifically impairs hair-cell exocytosis without any detectable impact on hair-cell mechanotransduction or presynaptic-calcium influx.
source: Overall, this functional assessment indicates that Dynole 34–2 specifically impairs hair-cell exocytosis without any detectable impact on hair-cell mechanotransduction or presynaptic-calcium influx.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional assessment data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transient Dynole 34–2 treatment (during 30 min neomycin exposure) resulted in no significant protection with a mean % hair-cell survival similar to DMSO-treated controls.
source: Like our isradipine experiments, for this transient Dynole 34–2 treatment, we observed no significant protection with a mean % hair-cell survival similar to DMSO-treated controls (Figure 2F, 5-6 dpf).
evidence: This is supported by neomycin survival data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Pretreatment with 2.5 µM Dynole 34–2 for 24 or 48 hr prior to neomycin treatment offered significant protection compared to DMSO controls.
source: However, pretreatment with 2.5 µM Dynole 34–2 for 24 or 48 hr prior to neomycin treatment offered significant protection compared to DMSO controls (Figure 2G-H, 5 dpf).
evidence: This is supported by neomycin survival data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: Prolonged loss (~24 hr) of neurotransmission reduces neomycin susceptibility.
source: Taken together, analysis of our mutant models and our pharmacology experiments suggest that prolonged loss (~24 hr) of neurotransmission reduces neomycin susceptibility.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutant and pharmacology data in Figure 2.

claim: Impairing the synaptic vesicle cycle even in the presence of normal calcium currents results in a level of neomycin resistance comparable to that observed in the absence of both calcium influx and exocytosis.
source: Surprisingly, impairing the synaptic vesicle cycle even in the presence of normal calcium currents results in a level of neomycin resistance comparable to that observed in the absence of both calcium influx and exocytosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing the protection in otofb mutants and Dynole-treated cells to cav1.3a mutants.

claim: The synaptic vesicle cycle contributes to hair-cell neomycin susceptibility.
source: This suggests that it is the synaptic vesicle cycle contributes to hair-cell neomycin susceptibility.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data comparing different manipulations of neurotransmission.

claim: After gentamicin treatment, significantly more surviving cells were found in both cav1.3a and otofb mutants relative to controls.
source: Using this approach, after gentamicin treatment, we found significantly more surviving cells in both cav1.3a and otofb mutants relative to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-F).
evidence: This is supported by gentamicin survival data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neurotransmission may impact the susceptibility of hair cells to a diverse range of ototoxins.
source: Together, our neomycin and gentamicin assays indicate that neurotransmission may impact the susceptibility of hair cells to a diverse range of ototoxins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the neomycin and gentamicin data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: No significant difference in Neo-TR intensity was observed between CaV1.3a- or Otofb-deficient hair cells and their respective sibling controls at the 10-min endpoint.
source: We observed no significant difference in the Neo-TR intensity between CaV1.3a- or Otofb-deficient hair cells and their respective sibling controls at the 10-min endpoint (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by Neo-TR uptake data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: No significant difference was observed between mutants and siblings at any timepoint during Neo-TR uptake.
source: We also observed no significant difference between mutants and siblings at any timepoint during Neo-TR uptake (Figure 3C and E).
evidence: This is supported by Neo-TR uptake kinetics data shown in Figure 3C and E.

claim: Lack of CaV1.3 channels or Otoferlin does not impair the ability of neomycin to enter hair cells.
source: These results indicate that lack of CaV1.3 channels or Otoferlin does not impair the ability of neomycin to enter hair cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Neo-TR uptake data in Figure 3.

claim: A decrease in Neo-TR signal was observed in both caV1.3a and otofb mutant hair cells after washout, but this decrease was not significantly different compared to sibling controls.
source: While we did observe a decrease in Neo-TR signal in both caV1.3a and otofb mutant hair cells, this decrease was not significantly different compared to sibling controls (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: This is supported by Neo-TR clearance data shown in Figure 3D and F.

claim: Similar Neo-TR clearance trajectories indicate that the protection in caV1.3a or otofb mutants is not due to augmented neomycin clearance.
source: Similar Neo-TR clearance trajectories indicate that the protection in in caV1.3a or otofb mutants is not due to augmented neomycin clearance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Neo-TR clearance data in Figure 3.

claim: Neo-TR rapidly forms puncta after uptake into hair cells.
source: After uptake into hair cells, Neo-TR rapidly forms puncta.
evidence: This is an observation from the Neo-TR imaging experiments.

claim: Neo-TR puncta co-label with the lysosomal markers LysoTracker green and GFP-Rab7.
source: Previous work in the lateral line has shown that these puncta co-label with the lysosomal markers LysoTracker green and GFP-Rab7 (Hailey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Loading of neomycin into lysosomes is proposed to be a protective measure.
source: Loading of neomycin into these lysosomes is proposed to be a protective measure.
evidence: This is based on prior work about lysosomal sequestration of aminoglycosides.

claim: The presence of bright puncta, indicative of Neo-TR sequestration within lysosomes, is apparent in both caV1.3a and otofb mutants.
source: The presence of bright puncta, indicative of Neo-TR sequestration within lysosomes, is apparent in both caV1.3a and otofb mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Neo-TR imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lack of gross differences in the observed pattern of formation of Neo-TR lysosomal puncta suggests that lack of CaV1.3 channels or Otoferlin does not offer protection through differential lysosomal loading.
source: The lack of gross differences in the observed pattern of formation of Neo-TR lysosomal puncta suggests that lack of CaV1.3 channels or Otoferlin does not offer protection through differential lysosomal loading.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Neo-TR imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The neomycin protection observed in CaV1.3- or Otofb-deficient hair cells is not due to altered Neo-TR uptake, clearance, or trafficking into lysosomes.
source: Taken together, our assays using Neo-TR indicate that the neomycin protection observed in CaV1.3- or Otofb-deficient hair cells is not due to altered Neo-TR uptake, clearance, or trafficking into lysosomes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the Neo-TR data in Figure 3.

claim: While all hair cells in each lateral-line neuromast are mechanosensitive, only a subset of cells exhibit neurotransmission when depolarized by mechanical stimuli.
source: Previous work by our group demonstrated while all hair cells in each lateral-line neuromast are mechanosensitive, only a subset of cells exhibit neurotransmission when depolarized by mechanical stimuli (Figure 1E–E', G–G'1–I'; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and data shown in Figure 1.

claim: After neomycin treatment, active hair cells exhibit significantly higher survival compared to inactive hair cells.
source: Surprisingly, after neomycin treatment, we observed that active hair cells exhibit significantly higher survival compared to inactive hair cells (example: Figure 4A–A''', quantification: Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by neomycin survival data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Within wildtype neuromasts, the presence of neurotransmission is associated with protection from neomycin.
source: This indicates that within wildtype neuromasts, the presence of neurotransmission is associated with protection from neomycin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data comparing active and inactive cells in Figure 4B.

claim: Older hair cells are thought to exhibit higher susceptibility to neomycin.
source: In addition, previous work has suggested that hair cells of different ages show differences in susceptibility to neomycin–namely that older hair cells are thought to exhibit higher susceptibility (Murakami et al., 2003; Pickett et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: At 3 dpf, DAPI is only taken up by functionally mature cells via mechanosensitive ion channels.
source: For DAPI labeling, we applied the vital dye at 3 dpf. At this stage, DAPI is only taken up by functionally mature cells via mechanosensitive ion channels.
evidence: This is based on the properties of DAPI labeling and mechanosensitive channel function.

claim: DAPI is retained in the same set of hair cells days after dye labeling.
source: Importantly, similar to previous work using Hoechst label, we observed that DAPI is retained in the same set of hair cells days after dye labeling (Pickett et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and the experimental observations.

claim: The presence of DAPI label at 5 dpf can distinguish older cells (DAPI-positive) from younger cells (DAPI-negative) that matured or were added to the neuromast after the initial DAPI labeling at 3 dpf.
source: Thus, the presence of DAPI label at 5 dpf can distinguish older cells (DAPI-positive) from younger cells (DAPI-negative) that matured or were added to the neuromast after the initial DAPI labeling at 3 dpf (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B').
evidence: This is supported by the DAPI labeling protocol and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kinocilial height is a useful way to stage hair cells developmentally.
source: Previous work has shown that kinocilial height is a useful way to stage hair cells developmentally (Kindt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The kinocilial heights of all DAPI-positive hair cells at 5 dpf were >20 µm, consistent with a mature population of hair cells.
source: After DAPI labeling at 3 dpf, we found that the kinocilial heights of all DAPI-positive hair cells at 5 dpf were >20 µm, consistent with a mature population of hair cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by kinocilial height measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DAPI-negative hair cells had a more even spread of kinocilial heights (2.5–23.5 µm), consistent with a developing population of hair cells.
source: In contrast DAPI-negative hair cells had a more even spread of kinocilial heights (2.5–23.5 µm), consistent with a developing population of hair cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by kinocilial height measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Either kinocilial height or DAPI labeling can be used to estimate hair-cell age.
source: Overall, these data indicate that either kinocilial height or DAPI labeling can be used to estimate hair-cell age.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the DAPI and kinocilial height data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: After application of 100 µM neomycin for 30 min, younger hair cells had significantly higher survival compared to mature hair cells.
source: After application of 100 µM neomycin for 30 min, we observed that younger hair cells had significantly higher survival compared to mature hair cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-E'; % of young cells surviving: 63.17%±8.62, % of mature cells surviving: 10.93%±3.16).
evidence: This is supported by neomycin survival data based on kinocilial height shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-E'.

claim: Within wildtype neuromasts, younger hair cells are less susceptible to neomycin.
source: This indicates that within wildtype neuromasts, younger hair cells are indeed less susceptible to neomycin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the neomycin survival data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-E'.

claim: Significantly more inactive cells were older and DAPI-positive compared to active cells (active: 22.5%, inactive 87.5% cells per neuromast DAPI-positive).
source: We found that significantly more inactive cells were older and DAPI-positive compared to active cells (Figure 4D–D''', Figure 4E; active: 22.5%, inactive 87.5% cells per neuromast DAPI-positive).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI labeling and functional imaging data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Within a given neuromast, active hair cells exhibiting evoked neurotransmission represent a younger population of hair cells compared to inactive hair cells.
source: Overall, our DAPI experiments revealed that within a given neuromast, active hair cells exhibiting evoked neurotransmission represent a younger population of hair cells compared to inactive hair cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the DAPI labeling data in Figure 4D-E.

claim: The relative youth of active hair cells helps to explain how hair cells with evoked neurotransmission are more resistant to neomycin despite evidence that chronic loss of neurotransmission is protective against neomycin.
source: Furthermore, their relative youth helps to explain how hair cells with evoked neurotransmission are more resistant to neomycin despite our evidence that chronic loss of neurotransmission is protective against neomycin.
evidence: This is an interpretation that reconciles the seemingly contradictory findings about active vs inactive cells and mutants.

claim: The lack of neurotransmission observed in older hair cells is consistent with the hypothesis that over time, activity-driven ATP synthesis in hair cells can lead to the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and induce cellular damage.
source: The lack of neurotransmission we observed in older hair cells was intriguing (Figure 4C–E). It is also consistent with the hypothesis that over time, activity-driven ATP synthesis in hair cells can lead to the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and induce cellular damage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in Figure 4 in the context of the overall hypothesis.

claim: Synaptic silencing in older cells could be a way to prevent ROS accumulation and associated pathology.
source: If neurotransmission is a driver of these metabolic demands, synaptic silencing in older cells could be a way to prevent ROS accumulation and associated pathology.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data.

claim: Significantly lower CellROX Orange baseline fluorescence was found in both caV1.3a and otofb mutant hair cells relative to controls.
source: We found significantly lower CellROX Orange baseline fluorescence in both caV1.3a and otofb mutant hair cells relative to controls (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is supported by CellROX Orange data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Significantly lower MitoSOX Red baseline fluorescence was found in caV1.3a and otofb mutant hair cells relative to controls.
source: Likewise, labeling using MitoSOX Red revealed significantly lower MitoSOX Red baseline fluorescence in caV1.3a and otofb mutant hair cells relative to controls (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This is supported by MitoSOX Red data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: The loss of neurotransmission in CaV1.3a or Otofb-deficient hair cells results in a lower baseline level of ROS accumulation and lower oxidative stress.
source: Together our CellROX Orange and MitoSOX Red measurements suggest that the loss of neurotransmission in CaV1.3a or Otofb-deficient hair cells results in a lower baseline level of ROS accumulation and lower oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CellROX and MitoSOX data in Figure 5.

claim: ROS impart damage to DNA, lipids, proteins, and many other molecules throughout the cell, rendering cells overall more susceptible to insults.
source: ROS are known to impart damage to DNA, lipids, proteins, and many other molecules throughout the cell, rendering cells overall more susceptible to insults (Yang and Lian, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Lower levels of baseline ROS could explain why caV1.3a and otofb mutant hair cells exhibit resistance to neomycin-induced cell death.
source: Therefore, lower levels of baseline ROS could explain why caV1.3a and otofb mutant hair cells exhibit resistance to neomycin-induced cell death.
evidence: This is a conclusion linking the ROS data to the neomycin survival data.

claim: CaV1.3a-deficient auditory hair cells in mice retain immature characteristics.
source: Work in mice has shown that CaV1.3a-deficient auditory hair cells in mice retain immature characteristics (Brandt et al., 2003; Eckrich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in mice.

claim: Mutations that impact hair-cell function in mice can not only impair development, but also lead to cell death.
source: In addition, mutations that impact hair-cell function in mice can not only impair development, but also lead to cell death (Schwander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work in mice.

claim: In the lateral line, hair cells regenerate after cell death, and the death of many hair cells may result in higher rates of cell turnover.
source: In the lateral line, hair cells regenerate after cell death, and the death of many hair cells may result in higher rates of cell turnover (Harris et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The same number of hair cells per neuromast was found in caV1.3a and otofb mutants compared to controls at both 3 and 5 dpf.
source: This analysis revealed the same number of hair cells per neuromast in caV1.3a and otofb mutants compared to controls at both ages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,E).
evidence: This is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,E.

claim: Similar cell counts suggest that both mutants generate hair cells at a normal rate and show no obvious loss of hair cells.
source: Similar cell counts suggest that both mutants generate hair cells at a normal rate and show no obvious loss of hair cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cell count data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,E.

claim: From 3 to 5 dpf, similar to controls, CaV1.3a and Otofb-deficient hair cells did not show a significant loss of DAPI-positive hair cells.
source: We found that from 3 to 5 dpf, similar to controls, CaV1.3a and Otofb-deficient hair cells did not show a significant loss of DAPI-positive hair cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,G).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI retention data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,G.

claim: In the lateral line, loss of CaV1.3a or Otofb does not result in more cell death or subsequently more cell turnover.
source: Our DAPI results indicate that in the lateral line, loss of CaV1.3a or Otofb does not result in more cell death or subsequently more cell turnover.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the DAPI retention data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,G.

claim: The average kinocilial height was not different between caV1.3a or otofb mutants compared to controls at 5 dpf.
source: We found that the average kinocilial height was not different between caV1.3a or otofb mutants compared to controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,F).
evidence: This is supported by kinocilial height measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,F.

claim: The average height of the kinocilium in young and mature hair cell populations was not different in caV1.3a or otofb mutants compared to controls.
source: After this split, we found that the average height of the kinocilium in young and mature hair cell populations was not different in caV1.3a or otofb mutants compared to controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, F).
evidence: This is supported by kinocilial height measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,F.

claim: Hair cells in caV1.3a and otofb mutants develop at a normal rate.
source: Our measurements of hair-bundle height suggest that hair cells in caV1.3a and otofb mutants develop at a normal rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinocilial height data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,F.

claim: CaV1.3a or Otofb-deficient hair cells mature at a relatively normal rate and show no evidence of increased cell death or turnover.
source: Overall, our assessment revealed that CaV1.3a or Otofb-deficient hair cells mature at a relatively normal rate and show no evidence of increased cell death or turnover.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the developmental assessment data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: CaV1.3a or Otofb-deficient hair cells accumulate less ROS due to the loss of neurotransmission rather than due to cellular immaturity.
source: These results support the conclusion that CaV1.3a or Otofb-deficient hair cells accumulate less ROS due to the loss of neurotransmission rather than due to cellular immaturity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the developmental assessment ruling out immaturity as an explanation.

claim: In both neurons and hair cells, presynaptic calcium influx can drive calcium into mitochondria.
source: In both neurons and hair cells, presynaptic calcium influx can drive calcium into mitochondria (Marland et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In neurons, calcium influx into mitochondria has been shown to stimulate oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria and contribute to metabolic stress.
source: Furthermore, in neurons, calcium influx into mitochondria has been shown to stimulate oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria and contribute to metabolic stress (Brookes et al., 2004; Tarasov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in neurons.

claim: When the lateral-line system matures (5 dpf), hair-cell stimulation drives calcium into mitochondria.
source: Previous work has shown that when the lateral-line system matures (5 dpf), hair-cell stimulation drives calcium into mitochondria (Pickett et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CaV1.3a-deficient hair cells exhibit an absence of evoked mitochondrial-calcium uptake during fluid-jet stimulation.
source: During fluid-jet stimulation, in mature hair cells at 5–6 dpf, we observed an absence of evoked mitochondrial-calcium uptake in CaV1.3a-deficient hair cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-B').
evidence: This is supported by mitoGCaMP3 data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-B'.

claim: Block of CaV1.3 channels with the antagonist isradipine inhibits mitochondrial-calcium uptake.
source: This is consistent with previous pharmacological results showing that block of CaV1.3 channels with the antagonist isradipine inhibits mitochondrial-calcium uptake (Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Otofb-deficient hair cells exhibit robust mitochondrial-calcium uptake during fluid-jet stimulation.
source: Interestingly, during fluid-jet stimulation, we observed robust mitochondrial-calcium uptake in Otofb-deficient hair cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C-C').
evidence: This is supported by mitoGCaMP3 data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C-C'.

claim: No significant difference was found in the peak evoked mitoGCaMP3 responses between otofb mutants and siblings.
source: We quantified the peak evoked mitoGCaMP3 responses in otofb mutants and siblings and found no significant difference (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C').
evidence: This is supported by mitoGCaMP3 data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C'.

claim: A reduction in evoked mitochondrial-calcium uptake is not a common factor leading to a reduction in neomycin susceptibility in Otofb- and CaV1.3a-deficient hair cells.
source: Overall, our mitoGCaMP3 measurements indicate that a reduction in evoked mitochondrial-calcium uptake is not a common factor leading to a reduction in neomycin susceptibility in Otofb- and CaV1.3a-deficient hair cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mitoGCaMP3 data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Calcium influx into mitochondria can stimulate oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria.
source: Although calcium influx into mitochondria can stimulate oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria, it is just one factor that contributes to mitochondrial function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential is the main driver of oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Therefore, we used TMRE and JC-1, vital dyes that have been used previously in neurons and hair cells to study mitochondrial membrane potential–this potential is the main driver of oxidative phosphorylation (Esterberg et al., 2016; Joshi and Bakowska, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: A significant reduction in TMRE baseline fluorescence was found in both caV1.3a and otofb mutant hair cells relative to their respective sibling controls.
